summaries.example: Think about a house made from boards, stones, and nails. The house is a whole, and the boards and stones are parts. But philosophers asked tricky questions: Is a house still the same house if one board is replaced? Is a crowd a whole in the same way a person is? These questions show why simply listing parts is not enough.
summaries.summary: Medieval mereology was the study of parts, wholes, and the ways they are connected. Medieval thinkers found ideas about these relationships in discussions of division and in a logical subject called the Topics. They considered many kinds of wholes: physical things such as houses and living beings, groups of individuals called universals, and things made up of powers, such as a soul with powers of thinking or sensing. They also asked whether a whole is just all its parts put together. Some philosophers said yes, while others argued that a whole can be more than its parts. These questions were connected to larger questions about what makes something one thing and whether it remains the same when parts change.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers studied parts and wholes in logic, philosophy, and theology.
They discussed different kinds of wholes, including physical objects, universals, and the powers of a soul.
A hand can be a part of a person, but a person is not simply the same thing as one hand.
They used these ideas to think about identity and about whether something stays the same after it changes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Questions about parts and wholes appear in everyday life. We wonder whether a repaired toy is still the same toy, or whether a person remains the same after growing and changing. Medieval philosophers developed careful ways to discuss such puzzles. Their work shows that old philosophical ideas can still help us ask clear questions about objects, living things, groups, and change.

important_terms.definition: The study of how parts and wholes are related.
Something made from, or divided into, other things.
Something that makes up or belongs to a whole.
A process of separating one unity into several items, or grouping items into a unity.

questions_to_think_about: If a bicycle loses one small piece, is it still the same bicycle?
Is a crowd a whole in the same way that a person is a whole?
Can something be a part of a whole without being a physical piece?
Why might a philosopher say that a person can lose a fingernail and still remain the same person?

summaries.example: Consider a living human being who loses a fingernail. The strict version of the claim “if the part is gone, the whole is gone” would suggest that the person no longer exists. Medieval philosophers recognized that this is too strong for many cases. They distinguished principal parts, whose loss may destroy a thing’s form, from secondary parts, whose loss need not destroy the thing. Yet they disagreed about how to identify those parts and about whether identity depends on the exact material components.
summaries.summary:
Medieval mereology examines parts, wholes, and the logical or metaphysical relations between them. Its main forums were discussions of division and the Topics, where philosophers sought principles that could support inferences about wholes and parts. A central problem was that “whole” could refer to several different structures. Integral wholes are composed of components, as a house is composed of materials or a body of bodily parts. Universal wholes, such as a species or genus, are related to individuals or subordinate universals, but they are not generally treated as literal collections of those items. Potential wholes, most notably the soul considered through its powers, have yet another structure: their powers are related to the whole’s capacities without being separable pieces.

These distinctions generated disputes. A universal and a collection may have many of the same individuals associated with them, so philosophers needed more precise criteria, including predication, dependence, quantity, and composition. They also disagreed about whether a composite is identical to its parts taken together. Mereology then became part of debates about identity and persistence. If a thing loses a part, does it cease to exist? Some thinkers distinguished principal parts from secondary parts; others explained persistence through a substantial form or through different senses of numerical sameness. The entry presents these debates as connected attempts to determine what counts as a whole, what counts as a part, and what kind of unity a thing possesses.
key_ideas: Medieval discussions of mereology were especially developed in treatments of division and the Topics, influenced strongly by Boethius.
Integral, universal, and potential wholes have different kinds of parts and different relations to their parts.
The distinction between a universal whole and an integral whole cannot be explained simply by listing what sorts of things are their parts.
Medieval philosophers debated whether an integral whole is identical with the sum of its parts or is something distinct from that sum.
Mereological theories were used to analyze identity at a time, puzzles about many overlapping objects, and persistence through change.
Some accounts appealed to substantial form or a principal part to explain why an object can survive the loss of some material parts.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mereology connects apparently simple questions—what belongs to what, and what makes something one thing—to major metaphysical issues. It helps explain why a living being may survive material change, why a universal is not obviously a crowd, and why a soul’s powers present a special case. The medieval debates also resemble later and contemporary questions about composition, identity, overlap, and persistence, showing how detailed analysis of part-whole relations can shape an entire theory of reality.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of parts, wholes, and the relations between them, in formal or informal terms.
A whole composed of spatial or material components, such as a body, house, or quantity of matter.
A whole related to individuals or subordinate universals, where the whole is predicated of each relevant part.
A whole understood through its powers or capacities, especially a soul and its faculties; it is not composed of parts as a house is.
A part that is a component of a whole’s matter or measurable size.
A part that helps constitute what a substance is, especially its matter or substantial form.
A part of a universal to which the universal’s name and definition can properly apply.
The continued existence or sameness of something through alteration over time.

questions_to_think_about: If a universal can exist even when no individual falls under it, how does it differ from a collection of individuals?
Can the same object be an integral whole in one respect and a substantial whole in another?
Does replacing a part create a new object, or can the original persist through the change?
What makes a power of the soul a part without making the soul a physical composite?
Is a whole ever more than the sum of its parts?

summaries.example: Imagine a school band. The band is made from musicians, but it is not the same kind of whole as one musician. If one musician leaves, the band may still exist, though it has changed. Now compare the idea “musician” as a general category. Each individual musician can be called a musician, but the category is not simply a pile of all musicians. Medieval philosophers used differences like these to ask whether groups, categories, and physical objects have parts in the same way.
summaries.summary:
Medieval mereology is the study of how parts and wholes are related. Philosophers approached it mainly through two logical subjects: division, which explains how a unity can be considered as many, and the Topics, which supplied general principles for reasoning. Boethius was especially important in transmitting these discussions to the medieval Latin world.

The medieval account did not treat every whole as the same kind of thing. An integral whole is composed from parts, as a body, house, or quantity may be. A universal whole is a genus or species related to the things that fall under it. A potential whole is understood through powers or capacities, such as the powers associated with a soul; its powers are not detachable pieces like boards from a house. These categories raised difficult questions. If every human individual is a part of the universal Human Being, is that universal just the total collection of humans? Some philosophers explored versions of that idea, while others argued that a universal depends on its individuals differently from an integral whole.

The topic also affected theories of identity. Medieval thinkers asked whether a composite whole is identical to the sum of its components, whether several overlapping arrangements create several objects, and whether a thing can survive the loss of a part. Proposed answers included distinctions between principal and secondary parts, between form and matter, and between strict and less strict senses of being numerically the same.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers found sustained discussions of parts and wholes in division and in the Topics.
They distinguished physical or integral wholes from universal wholes and potential wholes.
A universal is not automatically the same as a collection of all the individuals under it.
Philosophers disagreed about whether a whole is nothing more than its parts and about which changes destroy identity.
The study of parts and wholes was used to investigate living beings, souls, objects, identity, and change.
summaries.why_it_matters: Part-whole questions are useful far beyond medieval logic. They help us think about whether a team, machine, organism, or category remains the same when its members or materials change. Medieval philosophers also show that “part” can mean more than a physical piece: it can refer to a defining element, a capacity, or an individual falling under a general kind. Studying their distinctions makes everyday ideas about sameness and change more precise.

important_terms.definition: The study of parts, wholes, and the relations that connect them.
A whole whose components make it up, such as a house, body, or collection.
A general whole, such as a species or genus, that can be predicated of its members or subordinate kinds.
A whole understood as having powers or capacities, especially a soul and its powers.
A part that belongs to a whole because the whole’s name and definition apply to it.
A principle used in an argument; medieval logicians called especially basic principles “maximal propositions.”
The continued identity of something while it undergoes change.

questions_to_think_about: Is a sports team the same team after some players leave and new players join?
Why is a category such as “animal” different from a collection of all animals?
Could a mind or soul have parts even if it cannot be cut into physical pieces?
Which parts of a house are necessary for it to remain a house?
Should two overlapping objects count as two different objects?
